Lessons.Title: Organizing Data
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: select useful displays for paired measurements and explain what an observed pattern does or does not establish. One-variable bar charts and bivariate scatter plots answer different questions.

Use an original survey in which each of five plants has measured sunlight hours and growth height: (1,2),(2,4),(3,5),(4,7),(5,8). Each ordered pair must stay paired. Discuss whether the data appear positively associated and whether other influences, such as water, could matter.

Student task: choose axes and plot the five measurement pairs, then compare a two-variable scatter plot to separate unpaired summaries. A teacher checks axis units, retained pairings, and written reasoning; no automated correctness claim for self-collected data.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/1/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Bivariate observation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two measurements recorded for one subject.
KeyConcepts.Example: Plant A: 1 sunlight hour, 2 cm growth.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scatter plot
KeyConcepts.Definition: A display of paired numeric observations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Place each (x,y) at its measured coordinates.
KeyConcepts.Example: Plot plant (3,5) as a single point.

KeyConcepts.Title: Association
KeyConcepts.Definition: A pattern in how two variables vary together.
KeyConcepts.Example: Higher recorded sunlight often coincides with greater growth.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count paired observations
WorkedExamples.Question: A study lists five plant pairs. How many dots should a scatter plot contain?
WorkedExamples.Method: Each paired row represents one observation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Separating x and y summaries would lose pairing.

WorkedExamples.Title: Read one observation
WorkedExamples.Question: What does (4,7) mean when x is sunlight hours and y is growth centimeters?
Steps: Both belong to the same plant.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A plant with 4 hours sunlight and 7 cm growth.
WorkedExamples.Check: The pair is not two different plants.

WorkedExamples.Title: Describe trend
WorkedExamples.Question: For pairs (1,2),(2,4),(3,5),(4,7),(5,8), does y generally rise with x?
Steps: As x progresses from 1 to 5, y rises from 2 to 8.
Each successive measured y is larger.
This pattern is a positive association, not proof that sunlight alone caused growth.
WorkedExamples.Check: A confounding variable could still exist.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Losing the paired structure of measurements.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Unpaired displays cannot recover which observations belong together.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Store each subject as a complete (x,y) row.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming association proves cause.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Confounding variables or selection can create association.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe the observed pattern without unsupported causal claims.

SummaryPoints: Paired observations are the foundation of bivariate displays.
Graph both quantities on labeled axes.

Lessons.Title: Plotting Data
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: gather or use bivariate data and make a mathematically readable scatter plot, selecting axes with appropriate units and scales.

A class investigation might compare arm span and height, but personal measurements should not be published or shared outside the classroom without permission. An independent fictional sample is (140,139),(145,146),(150,149),(155,157) measured in centimeters.

Draw an original scatter plot with both axes measured in centimeters, appropriate scales, and no connecting line through separate pupils. If a student gathers real observations, the teacher reviews ethical data collection and accurate plotted pairs; do not submit personal class data to external services.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/2/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Axis meaning
KeyConcepts.Definition: An axis identifies variable and measurement unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Label with quantity and unit, e.g. height (cm).
KeyConcepts.Example: Point (150,149) means height 150 cm, arm span 149 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale selection
KeyConcepts.Definition: Tick labels convert grid distance to measured value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Include the full measured range and regular spacing.

KeyConcepts.Title: Independent plotted points
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each point is one subject’s two measurements.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not connect subjects in an artificial time sequence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret measured pair
WorkedExamples.Question: With x=height and y=arm span, interpret (150,149).
WorkedExamples.Answer: Height 150 cm and arm span 149 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: Swapping axes would change the reading.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count points
WorkedExamples.Question: Four students each provide one height-span pair. How many plotted observations?
Steps: For each, place the dot at its x and y.
WorkedExamples.Check: No extra dot is made for each individual measurement.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check swapped point
WorkedExamples.Question: A recorded pair is height 145, span 146. A dot at (146,145) is drawn. Is it correct?
Steps: x-axis represents height and should show 145.
y-axis represents span and should show 146.
The plotted pair swaps the values.
WorkedExamples.Check: Read labels before plotting.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Connecting unrelated subjects as a line graph.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: No time/order continuity is implied.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Exposing classmate measurements unnecessarily.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Some physical data are personal.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use permission and anonymous or fictional data as appropriate.

SummaryPoints: Label units and use meaningful scales.

Lessons.Title: What a Point in a Scatter Plot Means
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret individual points, comparisons and outliers in a scatter plot without confusing one observation with the trend of all points.
Each dot encodes two measured variables for one subject. A dot far from others may reflect an unusual subject or an error; one exceptional point does not by itself invalidate the rest.

Using fictional paired data (1,3),(2,5),(3,7),(4,9),(5,4), identify the dot that differs most from an upward linear pattern and explain what additional information should be checked. Teacher-scored reasoning addresses measurement uncertainty.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/3/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Point meaning
KeyConcepts.Definition: The same observation supplies both coordinates.
KeyConcepts.Example: (3,7) means x=3, y=7 for one case.

KeyConcepts.Title: Outlier candidate
KeyConcepts.Definition: A value noticeably away from a general cloud of points.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Inspect it, but do not delete automatically.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pattern versus case
KeyConcepts.Definition: One observation and group association are distinct.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use several points to identify trend.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four rising points do not force a fifth to fit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret point
WorkedExamples.Question: For axes hours and dollars, what does (3,7) describe?
Steps: Both measurements describe a single case.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Three hours associated with seven dollars.
WorkedExamples.Check: Neither coordinate is the observation count.

WorkedExamples.Title: Spot unusual point
WorkedExamples.Question: Given (1,3),(2,5),(3,7),(4,9),(5,4), which point is far below y=2x+1?
Steps: The measured value at x=5 is 4.
Difference 7 is much larger than that for the first four points.
WorkedExamples.Check: It is an outlier candidate, not automatically an error.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check data pair
WorkedExamples.Question: Does (4,9) agree with the rule y=2x+1?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a point’s x-coordinate as its index number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: x represents the axis variable.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Read axes before interpreting the dot.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Deleting outliers to make a trend look tidy.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Outliers may convey important valid observations.

SummaryPoints: A dot records one paired case.
Group trend differs from individual variability.

Lessons.Title: Fitting a Line to Data
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use a line as an approximate model for a scatter plot, rather than mechanically connecting all points or forcing every observation onto the line.

An approximate line of fit balances the overall upward or downward cloud and helps predict values. A least-squares fit is one possible method; Grade 8 reasoning can instead choose a sensible line by eye, cite points near it, and discuss its limitations.

For fictional pairs (1,4),(2,6),(3,8),(4,11),(5,12), draw y≈2x+2, compare positive and negative vertical deviations, and critique extrapolation outside measured x. A teacher reviews fit quality and justification.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/4/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Line of fit
KeyConcepts.Definition: A line summarizing a roughly linear association.
KeyConcepts.Rule: It need not pass through every point.

KeyConcepts.Title: Residual
KeyConcepts.Definition: Observed y minus predicted y at the same x.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A positive residual lies above a model line.

KeyConcepts.Title: Prediction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use fitted relation at an x value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: An estimate, not a guaranteed outcome.
KeyConcepts.Example: At x=6, y≈14 with the example line.

WorkedExamples.Title: Residual above line
WorkedExamples.Question: At (4,11), line y=2x+2 predicts what, and residual?
WorkedExamples.Check: Point is one unit above the line.

WorkedExamples.Title: Residual below line
WorkedExamples.Question: At (5,12), model y=2x+2 predicts what residual?
WorkedExamples.Answer: 0; the point is on the line.
WorkedExamples.Check: Not all other points must also lie exactly on it.

WorkedExamples.Title: Extend cautiously
WorkedExamples.Question: Line y≈2x+2 predicts y at x=6.
WorkedExamples.Check: x=6 lies just beyond data up to 5, so the prediction is an extrapolation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Connecting dots in collection order.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Separate observations are not successive vertices of one curve.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw a single trend line instead.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting modeled output as an exact measurement.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A fit includes residuals.

SummaryPoints: A line of fit summarizes a bivariate cloud.
Residuals quantify departures from the line.

Visuals.Title: Line prediction and residual
Visuals.Description: At x=4, the fit y=2x+2 predicts 10; observed 11 gives residual +1.

Lessons.Title: Describing Trends in Scatter Plots
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: distinguish positive, negative, weak and absent linear associations and describe the strength using scatter rather than just slope.

Association direction tells whether larger x generally coincides with larger or smaller y. Association strength concerns how tightly observations cluster around a pattern. A strong negative association is possible even though its slope is negative.
Sort original fictional patterns: (1,8),(2,6),(3,4),(4,2) has strong downward trend; (1,3),(2,7),(3,2),(4,8) has no obvious simple trend. Teacher review checks explanations and uncertainty.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/5/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Positive association
KeyConcepts.Definition: Larger x tends to coincide with larger y.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative association
KeyConcepts.Definition: Larger x tends to coincide with smaller y.

KeyConcepts.Title: Strength
KeyConcepts.Definition: Degree of clustering around a pattern.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Tighter cloud means stronger apparent association.
KeyConcepts.Example: All points on y=10−2x form perfect negative linear association.

WorkedExamples.Title: Negative slope sample
WorkedExamples.Question: For points (1,8),(2,6),(3,4),(4,2), what is slope?
WorkedExamples.Check: Every adjacent output falls by two.

WorkedExamples.Title: Positive example
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) have what trend?
Steps: As x increases by 1, y rises by 2.
All three points align on y=2x.
WorkedExamples.Check: A fitted slope of 2 is positive.

WorkedExamples.Title: Trend caution
WorkedExamples.Question: Do pairs (1,3),(2,7),(3,2),(4,8) show a clear monotonic sequence?
Steps: y first rises, then falls, then rises.
There is no consistent monotone pattern across adjacent points.
Do not assert a perfect increasing trend.
WorkedExamples.Check: More observations and a suitable model may be needed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating negative slope with weak association.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Direction and strength are separate properties.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inferring a universal rule from a small cloud.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Association estimates can be unstable for small samples.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the observed sample size and limitations.

SummaryPoints: Association is not a causal claim.

Visuals.Title: A negative linear trend
Visuals.Description: Original lesson-example input-output table. Each row uses y = -2x + 10. Plotting this relation, when required, is a separate graphical task.

Lessons.Title: The Slope of a Fitted Line
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret the numerical slope of a fitted line as an estimated change in one variable for a unit change in another, including context and units.

For a model relating study hours x to quiz score y, slope 4 points/hour means an estimated four-point increase per additional hour within the range studied; it does not promise the same gain for every student.
Use a fictional line through (1,54) and (4,66). Compute slope and intercept and discuss uncertainty from scatter. Teacher review assesses contextual language and limitations.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/6/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model slope
KeyConcepts.Definition: Change in fitted output per input unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model intercept
KeyConcepts.Definition: Predicted output at x=0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimated rate
KeyConcepts.Definition: A model trend, not an individual guarantee.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four expected points per study hour in this model.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute score slope
WorkedExamples.Question: Find slope through (1,54) and (4,66).
WorkedExamples.Check: Predicts an increase of four per hour.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find intercept
WorkedExamples.Question: Slope 4 and model point (1,54). Find b.
WorkedExamples.Check: The model is y=4x+50.

WorkedExamples.Title: Predict with caution
WorkedExamples.Question: Predict modeled score for 3 hours on y=4x+50.
WorkedExamples.Check: Individual outcomes may differ because data scatter.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating slope as guaranteed individual improvement.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The line is a fit to data, not a deterministic law.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Omitting outcome/input units.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Slope is a ratio, not just a number.

SummaryPoints: Slope of fit is a contextual estimated rate.

Lessons.Title: Observing More Patterns in Scatter Plots
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: recognize nonlinear patterns and clusters in bivariate data and avoid imposing a straight-line model when the cloud curves.
A scatter plot may form a U-shape, arc, or two separate clusters rather than a single linear trend. An overall slope near zero can hide a real nonlinear association.
Graph original points (−2,4),(−1,1),(0,0),(1,1),(2,4). Explain why they form a curved pattern and why a straight line would miss their structure. Teacher feedback checks the sketch and reasoning.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/7/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonlinear association
KeyConcepts.Definition: The variables vary systematically without constant linear slope.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cluster
KeyConcepts.Definition: A subgroup of points concentrated in one region.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two sets of similar heights may form separate groups.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model mismatch
KeyConcepts.Definition: An imposed line fails to describe curvature or clusters.
KeyConcepts.Example: Horizontal line y=2 misses both center and ends of a parabola.

WorkedExamples.Title: Curved point set
WorkedExamples.Question: What pattern do (−2,4),(−1,1),(0,0),(1,1),(2,4) suggest?
Steps: At −2 and 2 the outputs both equal 4.
The central output is 0; points lie on y=x².
WorkedExamples.Check: The rate is not constant across x.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute variable changes
WorkedExamples.Question: For y=x², changes from x=0→1 and 1→2 are what?
Steps: Unequal changes prove not linear over these equal steps.
WorkedExamples.Check: A constant-slope model cannot exactly fit all points.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a misleading single-line claim
WorkedExamples.Question: Can one horizontal line exactly contain all five points above?
Steps: A horizontal line requires all y values equal.
WorkedExamples.Check: Curved structure must be recognized.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming every association is linear.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Many relationships curve or form subgroups.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dismissing a pattern because linear correlation looks small.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Nonlinear patterns can have low linear correlation.

SummaryPoints: Curves and clusters require their own description.
Match model form to data shape.

Visuals.Title: U-shaped nonlinear association
Visuals.Description: The squared-input data do not have constant first differences.

Lessons.Title: Analyzing Bivariate Data
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: evaluate a bivariate data set through plots, trend, outliers and limitations, and use evidence to support a concise statistical conclusion.

A strong analysis identifies both variables, sample size, general direction, unusual observations and whether the conclusion concerns association or cause. Different scales and missing measurements can distort appearance.

Investigate five original points (1,3),(2,4),(3,7),(4,8),(5,9). Compute how y generally changes and identify that one rise is larger than others. A teacher reviews statistical explanation, not a single predetermined adjective.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/8/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Trend summary
KeyConcepts.Definition: A statement about overall change supported by points.
KeyConcepts.Example: y rises from 3 to 9 as x rises from 1 to 5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Variation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Observed points need not follow equal steps.

KeyConcepts.Title: Statistical caveat
KeyConcepts.Definition: An observation-based conclusion can be limited.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State sample size and confounding possibility.
KeyConcepts.Example: Five observations alone cannot establish causation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Endpoint rate
WorkedExamples.Question: Across (1,3) to (5,9), what average y increase per x?
WorkedExamples.Check: This is not the same as all local steps.

WorkedExamples.Title: Largest local rise
WorkedExamples.Question: For y sequence 3,4,7,8,9, which consecutive rise is greatest?
WorkedExamples.Check: Other rises are +1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check sample size
WorkedExamples.Question: How many paired observations are in the set?
Steps: Each x-y row is one observation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Ten individual numerical values make five paired cases.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing endpoint slope with each local slope.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Averages can conceal variation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show both overall and local changes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming strong causal evidence from a tiny sample.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Other variables and sampling uncertainty remain.

SummaryPoints: Analyze direction, variation and sample size.
State evidence rather than unsupported claims.

Visuals.Title: Rate of increase between two observations
Visuals.Description: Original lesson-example input-output table. Each row uses y = 1.5x + 1.5. Plotting this relation, when required, is a separate graphical task.

Lessons.Title: Looking for Associations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare two categorical variables using organized counts and relative frequencies to investigate whether proportions differ across groups.

For categorical bivariate data a two-way table preserves both classifications. If the proportion preferring an option differs substantially by group, that indicates an association; raw counts alone can mislead when groups have different sizes.
Original fictional table: Group A 12 choose bus, 8 walk; Group B 5 choose bus, 15 walk. Compute within-group proportions. Teacher review checks fairness of comparison and causal caution.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/9/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two-way table
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counts by combinations of two categories.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Rows and columns reflect the same observations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Relative frequency
KeyConcepts.Definition: Part of a group satisfying a category.

KeyConcepts.Title: Categorical association
KeyConcepts.Definition: Differing conditional proportions across groups.
KeyConcepts.Example: Bus preference 60% in A and 25% in B.

WorkedExamples.Title: Group A percentage
WorkedExamples.Question: 12 of 20 in A choose bus. What percent?

WorkedExamples.Title: Group B percentage
WorkedExamples.Question: 5 of 20 in B choose bus. What percent?
WorkedExamples.Check: Bus share differs from A.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare proportions
WorkedExamples.Question: How many percentage points apart are A and B bus shares?
WorkedExamples.Check: This is an association measure, not a causal explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using total across both groups when estimating within-group rate.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That answers a different conditional question.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Divide by the selected group size.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating different shares with causal effect.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Group characteristics or selection may confound.

SummaryPoints: Use two-way tables for categorical data.

Visuals.Title: Conditional percentage of a group
Visuals.Description: Divide by the full group count 20, not by another category.

Lessons.Title: Using Data Displays to Find Associations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: read two-way tables and segmented bar displays to decide whether categorical relationships show an association.
For two groups of unequal sizes, construct 100% stacked bars to normalize counts. If category segments occupy different proportions, that suggests association between group and response.

Use an original table: A 30 choose fruit and 10 choose cereal; B 12 choose fruit and 28 choose cereal. Predict each bar segment and compare. Teacher review assesses correctly labeled percent axes and context.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/10/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Segmented bar
KeyConcepts.Definition: Displays category shares summing to 100% within each group.

KeyConcepts.Title: Group total
KeyConcepts.Definition: Denominator for a conditional proportion.

KeyConcepts.Title: Between-group comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare equal-normalized percentages.

WorkedExamples.Title: Group A share
WorkedExamples.Question: Group A fruit 30, cereal 10. Fruit percent?
WorkedExamples.Check: Remaining cereal share is 25%.

WorkedExamples.Title: Group B share
WorkedExamples.Question: Group B fruit 12, cereal 28. Fruit percent?
WorkedExamples.Check: Cereal share 70%.

WorkedExamples.Title: Association magnitude
WorkedExamples.Question: Difference in fruit share: A 75%, B 30%.
WorkedExamples.Check: Groups have substantially different preference proportions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using unequal bar heights for a 100%-stacked graph.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: These bars represent proportions and must each span 100%.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing count sizes without group denominators.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Unequal group sizes can skew counts.

Lessons.Title: Gone In 30 Seconds
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: design a short timing investigation, collect paired observations and analyze variability without claiming that a small sample yields universal conclusions.

An original 30-second challenge can measure how many simple symbols a participant copies in each of two trials. Record trial 1 and trial 2 counts as a pair for each consenting learner; do not upload named class data. Discuss practice effect, measurement error and differences among learners.

Use fictional counts (10,12),(15,17),(20,21),(25,24) for worked analysis. Teachers review ethical collection, the scatter plot, and whether conclusions are appropriately qualified. One numerical rate cannot certify experimental design.

Independently authored Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/6/11/preparation.html . Publisher graphics, individual data sets and assessments are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated measures
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two values from the same participant.

KeyConcepts.Title: Change between trials
KeyConcepts.Definition: Second minus first for each participant.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Positive means improvement in this metric.

KeyConcepts.Title: Experiment limitation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A short class study with sampling and order effects.
KeyConcepts.Example: Practice effect may raise second-trial counts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute pair change
WorkedExamples.Question: Participant records (15,17) symbols in two trials. What change?
WorkedExamples.Check: An increase of two in 30 seconds.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mean change
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs (10,12),(15,17),(20,21),(25,24). Average second-first change?
WorkedExamples.Check: This average hides one participant’s decrease.

WorkedExamples.Title: Assess variability
WorkedExamples.Question: Do all four participants improve?
WorkedExamples.Check: Sample does not prove a universal practice effect.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mixing trial counts across participants.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That destroys repeated-measure pairing.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use one paired row per participant.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming second-trial improvements prove a universal skill effect.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Small sample and practice/order confounding remain.

SummaryPoints: Keep paired timing data private and labeled.
Teacher review is needed for experimental conclusions.
